grammar.note_en:
Spanish nouns name people, objects and places. They have a grammatical gender: masculine or feminine. Gender belongs to the word; it does not mean that an object is male or female. Learn each noun with its article, the small word before it. Un libro means “a book”; el libro means “the book”. Una llave means “a key”; la llave means “the key”. The indefinite articles un and una introduce one object; definite el and la identify the object in the situation. Context decides which is appropriate. A word ending in -o is often masculine and one ending in -a often feminine, but the chapter already gives an exception: la mano, “the hand”, is feminine despite -o. El papel is “the paper”; its masculine gender is learned with el, not predicted by its ending.

An adjective describes a noun. It agrees with that noun: rojo becomes roja with a feminine noun. El libro rojo means “the red book”; la llave roja means “the red key”. Pequeño similarly has the feminine pequeña. Grande and azul keep the same form for masculine and feminine singular nouns: una caja grande means “a large box”; una llave azul means “a blue key”. These descriptions normally follow their nouns here. Every phrase in this chapter is singular, referring to one person or object; plural forms come next.

A verb expresses an action or state. The subject is the person or thing doing that action or being described. The forms here are for one named person or one thing: Ana tiene una caja means “Ana has a box”; Luis mira la caja means “Luis looks at the box”. Tiene belongs to tener, mira to mirar, abre to abrir, busca to buscar and entra to entrar. Learn these particular forms from the scene; the other persons come later. Spanish present forms can describe what is happening now: Ana busca means “Ana searches” or “Ana is searching”. Spanish does not need a separate word corresponding to English “does” in a negative statement: no precedes the verb. La llave no abre la puerta means “The key does not open the door”.

Spanish uses two verbs where English often has “is”. Es identifies or describes in the chapter: La caja es grande, “The box is large”. Está locates: La caja está en la mesa, “The box is on the table”. Do not reduce this distinction to permanent versus temporary: the chapter contrasts description and location. Tiene means “has”, not “is”: Ana tiene una caja, “Ana has a box”.

En expresses a location, “in” or “on” according to the objects: en la caja is “in the box”; en la mesa is “on the table”. De connects things: la puerta de la sala means “the door of the room”. De plus el contracts to del: dentro del libro means “inside the book”. Dentro and fuera contrast inside and outside. Aquí points to “here”; allí to “there”, relative to the speaker. In mira a Ana, “looks at Ana”, a introduces the named person who is looked at. Do not add a before an ordinary object: mira el libro, “looks at the book”.

Questions have an opening ¿ as well as a closing ?. Qué asks “what”, quién asks “who” and dónde asks “where”. ¿Qué tiene Ana? means “What does Ana have?”; ¿Dónde está la llave de la sala? means “Where is the reading room key?” The written accents are part of these question words. Y means “and”; pero means “but”, joining a contrast. Read the whole response to establish the intended object: a key that opens the box need not open the room.

The table also uses La caja está en la mesa, “The box is on the table”; el papel, “the paper”; and la mano, “the hand”. Read these as complete noun phrases with their articles. The arrow in a practice cue asks you to change the phrase, not to assert that a hypothetical red box is the story’s brown box.

Un papel means “a paper” or “a piece of paper”; una mano means “a hand”. Luis tiene una llave roja means “Luis has a red key”. These noun phrases show masculine un/el versus feminine una/la.
